newsitem.title: INDONESIA: African coffee producers' reforms bear fruit.
newsitem.headline: African coffee producers' reforms bear fruit.

text.p: Reforms to diversify the economies of African coffee-producing countries are beginning to bear fruit, increasing their capacity to withstand price volatility, their spokesman said on Wednesday.
Donald Kaberuka, chief economist at the 25-member InterAfrican Coffee Organisation (IACO), said the reforms aimed to lay the foundation for further diversification.
"The deep-seated reforms undertaken by the African countries in the last five years have been very promising. They are beginning to bear fruit," he told Reuters.
"Some of these countries are undergoing fundamental sectoral changes, including in coffee," he said. "We now need to consolidate these reforms."
Kaberuka said reforms had led to an increase in productivity and improved management of market risks.
He said, however, that although the reforms had raised the countries' capacity to withstand price turbulence, they were still sensitive to coffee prices in international markets.

"African countries still depend on coffee as a major foreign revenue earner," he said on the island of Bali, where he was attending a three-day meeting of the International Coffee Organisation (IACO) which ended on Wednesday.
He said African coffee-producing countries that had launched reforms included Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania.
The IACO led a move to get the world's top coffee producers to reduce exports in the first half of this year in a bid to bolster prices.

The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) decided at a meeting in Brazil on January 23 to reduce members' exports by 1.3 million 60-kg bags, in addition to an existing export ceiling of 26.28 million bags between January and June this year.
The ACPC said robusta coffee producers would cut exports by one million bags, and arabica growing countries the remainder.
Robusta coffee is known for its bitter flavour and is mixed with the more expensive arabica in portions that are considered a trade secret. African countries essentially produce robusta.
The IACO, in a country profile released on Tuesday, said the coffee industry in Uganda had been fully liberalised.
"Farmers now obtain a premium for quality, and quality aspects are carefully monitored at each part of the marketing chain," it said.
"Although the overwhelming dependence on coffee for the earning of foreign exchange has been moderately reduced, it still contributes the majority of export revenues," the report said.
Kaberuka said members of the IACO accounted for some 55 to 60 percent of global robusta production, with members including key producers such as Uganda, the Ivory Coast, Ethiopia and Kenya.
He said there was a need for Asian robusta producer Vietnam to join the ACPC as it could gain from international exposure.
Vietnam, which has said it cannot afford to join the organisation at present, has been privately criticised for not joining.
By staying out of the ACPC, Vietnam is not bound by the group's export limitation programmes but enjoys the benefits of such moves, critics say.
